name: Radix-two Cooley–Tukey discrete Fourier transform
definition: For N=2M=2^m (m≥1) and W_N=e^(−2πi/N), E_k=Σ_(n=0)^(M−1)x_(2n)W_M^(nk), O_k=Σ_(n=0)^(M−1)x_(2n+1)W_M^(nk); X_k=E_k+W_N^k O_k and X_(k+M)=E_k−W_N^k O_k for k=0,…,M−1, recursively to length 1.
variables: N=2^m transform length; M=N/2; x_n complex input; k frequency index; W_q=e^(−2πi/q); E_k and O_k even- and odd-index length-M transforms.
assumptions: Positive power-of-two N, with N=1 the identity base case; finite complex input; negative-exponent forward DFT with no forward normalization. The source uses the opposite sign, related by conjugating input and output.
limitations: This radix-two recurrence applies directly only when N is a power of two. Floating-point round-off, memory layout, bit-reversal order and speed depend on implementation and hardware; no sports forecasting benefit is established.
failure_conditions: N is not a positive power of two for this recurrence
Input contains non-finite values or arithmetic overflows
Implementation indexing, twiddle factors or output ordering are inconsistent with the declared DFT convention
computation: Recursively compute transforms of the even and odd subsequences, then combine each pair with one twiddle factor using the stated butterfly equations. For N=2^m this yields O(N log2 N) arithmetic; the exact operation count depends on the counting convention.

source.citation: Cooley, J. W. and Tukey, J. W. (1965). An algorithm for the machine calculation of complex Fourier series. Mathematics of Computation, 19(90), 297–301. https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1965-0178586-1

application: Numerical preprocessing or frequency-domain analysis of suitable time-series measurements in sporting contexts. This is a transform algorithm, not a forecast model; no predictive value is claimed.
required_inputs: Finite complex vector of length N=2^m and the declared DFT sign and normalization convention.
incompatible_methods: Non-power-of-two length when using this radix-two recurrence
mechanism_note: Split the direct DFT sum into even and odd input indices, use W_N²=W_M and W_N^M=−1. The two outputs share their length-M subtransforms. The recurrence T(N)=2T(N/2)+O(N) gives O(N log N). The original paper treats general sparse-factor FFTs and radix two; this is the canonical mechanism here, not a distinct algorithm for each radix.

name: Bluestein chirp convolution discrete Fourier transform
definition: For X_k=Σ_(n=0)^(N−1)x_n e^(−2πink/N), use 2nk=n²+k²−(k−n)² to obtain X_k=e^(−πik²/N)Σ_(n=0)^(N−1)[x_n e^(−πin²/N)]e^(+πi(k−n)²/N), a chirp-weighted linear convolution.
variables: N positive DFT length; n input index; k output index; x_n input; a_n=x_n e^(−πin²/N); b_r=e^(+πir²/N) for r=−(N−1),…,N−1.
assumptions: N is a positive integer; finite complex input; negative-exponent unnormalized forward DFT. For L≥2N−1 use a length-L circular embedding: a[n]=0 beyond n=N−1, b[0]=1, b[r]=b[L−r]=e^(+πir²/N) for 1≤r≤N−1, and zero otherwise. Use inverse FFT normalization consistently.
limitations: The convolution implementation requires correct negative-index embedding and padding. Floating-point error, memory use and speed depend on L and the selected FFT; this can cost more than a radix-two FFT when N already has favorable factors. No sports forecasting benefit is established.
failure_conditions: Padding length is less than 2N−1 or negative convolution indices are embedded incorrectly, causing circular aliasing
Chirp signs or FFT normalization do not match the declared DFT convention
computation: Compute the length-L circular convolution of the two explicitly embedded arrays with FFT and inverse FFT; for 0≤k<N, only differences k−n in [−(N−1),N−1] occur. Multiply each of these outputs by e^(−πik²/N). Choosing an FFT-supported L proportional to N gives O(N log N) arithmetic. A full ordinary linear convolution of lengths N and 2N−1 would instead require length at least 3N−2.

source.citation: Bluestein, L. I. (1970). A linear filtering approach to the computation of discrete Fourier transform. IEEE Transactions on Audio and Electroacoustics, 18(4), 451–455. https://doi.org/10.1109/TAU.1970.1162132

application: Computing the DFT for arbitrary-length sequences through chirp convolution, including preprocessing or frequency-domain analysis of suitable sporting time series. This is a transform algorithm, not a forecast model; no predictive value is claimed.
required_inputs: Finite complex vector of length N, DFT sign and normalization convention, and an FFT implementation with a supported padded length L≥2N−1.
incompatible_methods: FFT embedding that cannot preserve the required linear-convolution range or declared transform convention
mechanism_note: The quadratic identity 2nk=n²+k²−(k−n)² directly gives the chirp factorization. The length-L embedding represents every required signed difference uniquely modulo L; the first N circular outputs therefore equal the needed linear-convolution values. The original IEEE abstract confirms chirp filtering and O(N log N) for arbitrary length; full paper was not inspected.

name: Orthonormal discrete cosine transform type II
variables: N positive vector length; n input index; k coefficient index; x real vector; C cosine coefficients; α normalization
assumptions: Finite real vector with N≥1; all indices run from 0 to N−1; basis corresponds to an even extension about the half-sample boundaries
limitations: Full transform is invertible but truncating coefficients loses information. Energy compaction depends on the input; boundaries and sample ordering affect interpretation. No computational speedup or forecasting benefit is guaranteed
failure_conditions: Incorrect coefficient normalization, transform type or inverse
Inconsistent indexing or interpretation of extension boundaries
computation: Evaluate the orthonormal basis matrix times x directly in O(N²), or use a correctly normalized DCT implementation. The inverse is its transpose.

source.citation: SciPy v1.11.4 Manual, Fourier Transforms, Discrete Cosine and Sine Transforms. https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-1.11.4/tutorial/fft.html

application: General real-valued signal representation or compression; no forecast or predictive benefit is claimed.
required_inputs: Finite real vector, coefficient convention and sample ordering
incompatible_methods: Substitution of an unrelated sine or cosine boundary convention without adjusting the inverse
mechanism_note: Cosine product-to-sum and the finite sum of cos(π(n+1/2)m/N), which vanishes for integer m from 1 to 2N−1, give row norms N for k=0 and N/2 otherwise before scaling. Thus the matrix is orthogonal. This specifies a basis transformation, not a new FFT implementation.

name: Orthonormal discrete sine transform type I
variables: N number of interior samples; n and k are one-based indices; x real vector; S sine coefficients
assumptions: Finite real vector with N≥2 for compatibility with the cited implementation; zero boundary values at indices 0 and N+1 describe the odd extension
limitations: A nonzero physical boundary requires a suitable lifting or other basis if used for a boundary problem. Dropping coefficients loses information. No forecast benefit is claimed
failure_conditions: Wrong indexing, endpoint extension or scaling
Applying homogeneous boundary interpretation to an unadjusted nonhomogeneous problem
computation: Apply the normalized sine matrix directly in O(N²) or a matching DST-I routine. The inverse is the same matrix.

source.citation: SciPy v1.11.4 Manual, Fourier Transforms, Discrete Cosine and Sine Transforms. https://docs.scipy.org/doc/scipy-1.11.4/tutorial/fft.html

application: Represent finite real vectors or discretized functions with homogeneous endpoint conditions; no empirical application is asserted.
required_inputs: Finite real interior vector, sample ordering and endpoint convention
incompatible_methods: Using the DCT-II inverse or an incompatible sine-transform normalization
mechanism_note: The sine product-to-sum identity and the finite roots-of-unity sum on 2(N+1) points give Σ_(n=1)^N sin(πnk/(N+1))sin(πnl/(N+1))=(N+1)δ_kl/2. The scaled matrix is symmetric orthogonal and self-inverse. This is a feature transformation with a different boundary basis, not a new FFT algorithm.
